questions.stem: A 74-year-old man has had a weak urine stream and gets up three times a night to urinate for 2 years. Eight days ago he started several new medicines: ibuprofen for knee pain, lisinopril for blood pressure, diphenhydramine for itchy skin, hydrochlorothiazide for ankle swelling and omeprazole for heartburn. For 2 days he has had lower abdominal pain and passes only small amounts of urine. Blood pressure is 150/88 mm Hg. A tender, firm mass rises from the pelvis to just below the umbilicus. BUN is 54 mg/dL and creatinine is 3.0 mg/dL (1.1 mg/dL last month). Ultrasound shows hydronephrosis of both kidneys. A urinary catheter drains 1,400 mL of urine. Which of his new medicines most likely caused this kidney injury?
choices: Ibuprofen
Lisinopril
Diphenhydramine
Hydrochlorothiazide
Omeprazole
questions.explanation: A distended bladder, **bilateral hydronephrosis** and a large catheter volume show **postrenal AKI** from acute **urinary retention**. Diphenhydramine, a first-generation H1 blocker, is also **antimuscarinic**: it weakens M3-mediated **detrusor contraction**, and in a man with prostate enlargement this can stop bladder emptying. Ibuprofen and lisinopril are tempting because they cause AKI by changing glomerular arteriole tone, but that is a hemodynamic injury with no bladder distension or hydronephrosis. Omeprazole causes interstitial nephritis, which does not block urine flow.
questions.explanation_pt: Bexiga distendida, **hidronefrose bilateral** e grande volume drenado pela sonda mostram **LRA pós-renal** por **retenção urinária** aguda. A difenidramina, um anti-H1 de primeira geração, também é **antimuscarínica**: enfraquece a **contração do detrusor** mediada por receptores M3, e num homem com aumento da próstata isso pode impedir o esvaziamento da bexiga. Ibuprofeno e lisinopril são tentadores porque causam LRA ao alterar o tônus das arteríolas glomerulares, mas essa é uma lesão hemodinâmica, sem distensão vesical nem hidronefrose. O omeprazol causa nefrite intersticial, que não bloqueia o fluxo de urina.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man was admitted 2 weeks ago with septic shock from pneumonia. He developed acute tubular necrosis, and for 6 days he passed less than 400 mL of urine per day. He now passes about 4.5 L of urine per day. He takes no lithium or diuretics. His lab values today are: serum sodium 141 mEq/L, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, magnesium 1.4 mg/dL (normal 1.7-2.2), calcium 9.0 mg/dL, glucose 104 mg/dL, and creatinine 3.4 mg/dL (5.1 mg/dL five days ago). Urine osmolality is 290 mOsm/kg, and the urine has no glucose. Which of the following best explains his large urine output?
choices: Central diabetes insipidus from septic brain injury
Osmotic diuresis from glucose in the tubular fluid
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from high calcium
Excess free water intake caused by ICU thirst
New tubular cells unable to concentrate urine
questions.explanation: This is the **polyuric recovery phase of ATN**. The tubules are lined by **new, immature epithelial cells** that cannot yet build a concentrated urine or reabsorb salt well, while retained urea and salt are excreted. Urine osmolality near plasma (about 290) fits this, and losses of **potassium** and **magnesium** are typical. Central diabetes insipidus (and excess water intake) are tempting, but they give a very dilute urine (well below plasma osmolality), not urine close to plasma. Glucose and calcium are normal, so osmotic diuresis and hypercalcemic nephrogenic diabetes insipidus do not fit.
questions.explanation_pt: Esta é a **fase poliúrica de recuperação da NTA**. Os túbulos estão revestidos por **células epiteliais novas e imaturas**, que ainda não concentram a urina nem reabsorvem bem o sal, enquanto a ureia e o sal retidos são excretados. A osmolalidade urinária próxima à do plasma (cerca de 290) é compatível, e as perdas de **potássio** e **magnésio** são típicas. O diabetes insípido central (e a ingestão excessiva de água) são tentadores, mas produzem urina muito diluída (bem abaixo da osmolalidade plasmática), e não urina próxima à do plasma. Glicose e cálcio estão normais, então diurese osmótica e diabetes insípido nefrogênico por hipercalcemia não se encaixam.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman is in the intensive care unit with septic shock from a perforated colon. Her blood pressure stayed low for about 8 hours before it improved with fluids and vasopressors. Two days later her urine output is low. Lab values are: serum sodium 136 mEq/L, BUN 38 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 3.2 mg/dL; urine sodium 58 mEq/L, urine creatinine 40 mg/dL, and urine osmolality 310 mOsm/kg. Urine microscopy shows many granular casts. The kidney injury is most likely most severe in which part of the nephron?
choices: Straight proximal tubule, outer medulla
Glomerular capillary loops in the cortex
Distal convoluted tubule in the cortex
Thin descending limb in the inner medulla
Collecting duct at the tip of the papilla
questions.explanation: FENa is (58 × 3.2) / (136 × 40) × 100 ≈ **3.4%**, the BUN:creatinine ratio is about 12, and the urine is not concentrated: this is **ischemic ATN**. The **outer medulla** has low oxygen tension, and the **straight (S3) segment of the proximal tubule** and the medullary **thick ascending limb** use a lot of energy for active transport, so they die first. The thin descending limb is tempting because it lies in an even less oxygenated region, but it does almost no active transport and needs little oxygen.
questions.explanation_pt: A FENa é (58 × 3,2) / (136 × 40) × 100 ≈ **3,4%**, a relação BUN (nitrogênio ureico):creatinina é cerca de 12 e a urina não está concentrada: trata-se de **NTA isquêmica**. A **medula externa** tem baixa tensão de oxigênio, e o **segmento reto (S3) do túbulo proximal** e o **ramo ascendente espesso** medular gastam muita energia com transporte ativo, por isso morrem primeiro. O ramo descendente fino é tentador porque fica numa região ainda menos oxigenada, mas quase não faz transporte ativo e precisa de pouco oxigênio.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had tension headaches for many years. For over 10 years she has taken large amounts of over-the-counter pain tablets that contain an NSAID almost every day. Today she has sudden, colicky pain in her right flank and red urine. While urinating, she passes a small piece of gray tissue. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). Serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. The urine culture is negative, and the blood eosinophil count is normal. CT urography shows contrast in clefts at the tips of several renal papillae. Which mechanism best explains her kidney injury?
choices: Type IV hypersensitivity in the renal interstitium
Immune complex deposits in glomerular capillaries
Drug crystals that precipitate inside the tubules
Medullary ischemia from prostaglandin inhibition
Direct toxic necrosis of proximal tubule cells
questions.explanation: Colicky flank pain, **gross hematuria** and passage of tissue after years of heavy analgesic use point to **renal papillary necrosis**. The papillae get their blood from the vasa recta and depend on **prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation**; NSAIDs block this, so the papillae become **ischemic** and slough. NSAIDs can also cause **acute interstitial nephritis**, the tempting choice, but that gives pyuria and WBC casts, often with eosinophilia, and no sloughed tissue.
questions.explanation_pt: Dor lombar em cólica, **hematúria macroscópica** e eliminação de tecido após anos de uso intenso de analgésicos indicam **necrose de papila renal**. As papilas recebem sangue dos vasos retos (*vasa recta*) e dependem da **vasodilatação mediada por prostaglandinas**; os AINEs bloqueiam esse efeito, e as papilas ficam **isquêmicas** e descamam. Os AINEs também podem causar **nefrite intersticial aguda**, a alternativa tentadora, mas ela produz piúria e cilindros leucocitários, muitas vezes com eosinofilia, e não eliminação de tecido.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has chronic kidney disease from long-standing hypertension. He has felt more tired over the past year. He has no bleeding, and his stool test for blood is negative. His lab values are: hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 89 fL, reticulocytes 0.5%, normal ferritin and transferrin saturation, and normal vitamin B12 and folate. His estimated GFR is 18 mL/min/1.73 m2. Loss of which cells most directly explains his anemia?
choices: Juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole
Peritubular interstitial cells of the cortex
Proximal tubule cells that activate vitamin D
Macula densa cells of the distal tubule
Mesangial cells inside the glomerulus
questions.explanation: A **normocytic** anemia with a **low reticulocyte count** and normal iron, B12 and folate in advanced CKD is due to low **erythropoietin**. EPO is made by **peritubular interstitial (fibroblast-like) cells** of the renal cortex in response to low oxygen delivery, and these cells are lost as the kidney scars. Juxtaglomerular cells are the tempting choice because they are the best-known hormone-secreting cells of the kidney, but they release **renin**, not EPO. Proximal tubule cells make calcitriol, which explains the bone disease of CKD, not the anemia.
questions.explanation_pt: Uma anemia **normocítica** com **reticulócitos baixos** e ferro, B12 e folato normais na DRC avançada se deve à **eritropoetina** baixa. A EPO é produzida por **células intersticiais peritubulares (semelhantes a fibroblastos)** do córtex renal em resposta à baixa oferta de oxigênio, e essas células se perdem à medida que o rim fica fibrosado. As células justaglomerulares são a alternativa tentadora por serem as células secretoras de hormônio mais conhecidas do rim, mas liberam **renina**, e não EPO. As células do túbulo proximal produzem calcitriol, o que explica a doença óssea da DRC, e não a anemia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has end-stage kidney disease from diabetes. She has refused dialysis. One day after a tooth was removed, the socket still oozes blood, and she has new bruises on her arms. She had two dental extractions in her 30s without any bleeding problem, and no family members have a bleeding disorder. Her lab values are: platelet count 230,000/mm3, prothrombin time 12 seconds (normal), activated partial thromboplastin time 31 seconds (normal), BUN 110 mg/dL, and creatinine 8.2 mg/dL. A platelet function test shows a prolonged closure time. Which of the following best explains her bleeding?
choices: Low hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors
Autoantibodies that destroy circulating platelets
Inherited deficiency of von Willebrand factor
Uremic toxins that impair platelet adhesion
Consumption of clotting factors in small vessels
questions.explanation: A normal platelet count, normal PT and aPTT and a **prolonged platelet function test** in a patient with severe **uremia** point to **uremic platelet dysfunction**: retained toxins impair platelet **adhesion** to vessel walls and **aggregation**. Inherited von Willebrand disease is the tempting choice because it also causes mucosal bleeding with a normal platelet count, but she had no bleeding with earlier extractions and has no family history. Vitamin K deficiency and DIC would prolong the PT, and immune platelet destruction would lower the platelet count.
questions.explanation_pt: Contagem de plaquetas normal, TP e TTPa normais e **teste de função plaquetária prolongado** numa paciente com **uremia** grave indicam **disfunção plaquetária urêmica**: as toxinas retidas prejudicam a **adesão** das plaquetas à parede do vaso e a **agregação**. A doença de von Willebrand hereditária é a alternativa tentadora porque também causa sangramento mucoso com plaquetas normais, mas ela não sangrou em extrações anteriores e não tem história familiar. A deficiência de vitamina K e a CIVD prolongariam o TP, e a destruição imune de plaquetas reduziria a contagem plaquetária.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man comes to the clinic for the first time in 15 years. For several months he has felt tired and has had itchy skin. He has had high blood pressure readings at pharmacy checks but takes no medicines. Blood pressure is 172/104 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 6.1 mg/dL and BUN is 84 mg/dL. He has no earlier lab results. Which additional finding would most strongly suggest that his kidney disease has been present for a long time rather than a few days?
choices: Muddy brown granular casts in the urine
Fractional excretion of sodium above 2%
Serum potassium level of 6.0 mEq/L
Both kidneys dilated with hydronephrosis
Both kidneys small, with a thin cortex
questions.explanation: **Small kidneys with a thin, often echogenic cortex** show loss of nephrons and scarring over months to years, so they point to **chronic kidney disease**. Hyperkalemia is the tempting choice because it is common in CKD, but it also develops quickly in oliguric AKI, so it does not tell how long the disease has been present. Muddy brown casts and a FENa above 2% suggest **acute** tubular necrosis, and bilateral hydronephrosis suggests obstruction, which can be acute.
questions.explanation_pt: **Rins pequenos, com córtex fino e muitas vezes hiperecogênico**, mostram perda de néfrons e fibrose ao longo de meses a anos, e por isso indicam **doença renal crônica**. A hipercalemia é a alternativa tentadora porque é comum na DRC, mas também surge rapidamente na LRA oligúrica, e não informa há quanto tempo a doença existe. Cilindros granulosos marrom-escuros e FENa acima de 2% sugerem **necrose tubular aguda**, e a hidronefrose bilateral sugere obstrução, que pode ser aguda.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and large ascites is admitted with confusion. Over 5 days his serum creatinine rises from 1.0 to 2.5 mg/dL. His diuretics are stopped and he receives intravenous albumin for 2 days, but the creatinine does not improve. He has taken no NSAIDs, contrast or nephrotoxic antibiotics. Blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Urine sodium is 8 mEq/L and the fractional excretion of sodium is 0.1%. Urinalysis shows no protein, blood or casts. Ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis. Which mechanism best explains his kidney injury?
choices: Ischemic death of tubular epithelial cells
Immune complex deposits in the glomeruli
Renal vasoconstriction from splanchnic vasodilation
Hypersensitivity inflammation of the renal interstitium
Compression of both ureters by tense ascites
questions.explanation: This is **hepatorenal syndrome**. In **cirrhosis**, vasodilators such as nitric oxide widen the **splanchnic arteries**, and the low effective arterial volume activates the **renin-angiotensin**, sympathetic and ADH systems, which strongly constrict the renal arteries. The kidneys themselves are structurally normal, so the urine sodium is very low, the sediment is bland and the injury does not improve with albumin. ATN is the tempting choice in a hypotensive patient, but it gives granular casts and a FENa above 2%.
questions.explanation_pt: Esta é a **síndrome hepatorrenal**. Na **cirrose**, vasodilatadores como o óxido nítrico dilatam as **artérias esplâncnicas**, e o baixo volume arterial efetivo ativa os sistemas **renina-angiotensina**, simpático e do ADH, que contraem intensamente as artérias renais. Os rins em si são estruturalmente normais, por isso o sódio urinário é muito baixo, o sedimento é inocente e a lesão não melhora com albumina. A NTA é a alternativa tentadora num paciente hipotenso, mas produz cilindros granulosos e FENa acima de 2%.
